The US gross national debt reached $40tn for the first time on Wednesday, the highest in US history. The government deficit doubled over the past decade, with government spending growing under both Donald Trump and Joe Biden – Trump approved $8.4tn worth of debt during his first term, with a large chunk going to Covid-19 relief spending, while Biden approved $4.3tn worth of debt. In fiscal year 2026, which began in October 2025, $1.8tn has been added to the debt so far. Both Democrats and Republicans responded to the milestone with outrage, with Democrats placing the blame on Trump and a Republican-controlled Congress for the uptick in spending. “The President said he’d pay off the debt in his first term. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/books/out-o.text: The Budapest Times “Exploring Crime Fiction, Georges Simenon’s Normandy Coast Mysteries” by Bill Alder (published by Routledge) Out of the big bad city and beside the seaside Written by Christopher Osterberg Certain writers are synonymous with place – Dickens and London, Hardy with Wessex (Dorset), Maugham with the Far East and South Seas, Joyce with Dublin, Márquez and Colombia, Chandler/LA, Leonard/Detroit and so on. As Bill Alder points out, although Georges Simenon is often strongly associated with the French capital Paris, it isn’t as simple as that – let’s not forget his frequent ventures into Normandy. Alder’s reading of the 75 novels and 28 short stories featuring Chief Inspector Jules Maigret of the Police Judiciaire generally finds the streetwise detective in interior settings such as a comfortable bourgeois house in Neuilly or a brothel in Pigalle, and exterior locations like the Champs Elysées in the sun or a grey and rainy Canal Saint-Martin. But, Alder notes, of these 103 tales published between 1931 and 1972, 21 of the novels and 12 of the short stories take place away from the capital. That’s 33, very nearly a third. And it is the northern coastal region of Normandy that holds a prominent place among Maigret’s ventures outside Paris. Three novels are set entirely there (“Au Rendez-vous de Terre-Neuvas”/”The Grand Banks Café”, “Le Port des brumes”/”The Misty Harbour” and “Maigret et la vieille dame”/”Maigret and the Old Lady”), so is about a third of the action of a fourth book (“Pietr-le-Letton”/”Pietr the Latvian”), as well as two short stories (“La vieille dame de Bayeux” /”The Old Lady from Bayeux” and “Tempête sur la Manche”/”Storm over the Channel”). This puts Normandy alongside the Loire Valley and the Île de France as the most often used provincial settings for Maigret’s investigations, and thus it is this northern coastal region of France that is the focus of Alder’s book. To the delight of Simenon aficionados who’ve read a good deal of those 103 stories, and want to know more about their background, Alder has followed in the footsteps of the author and his popular creation to seek out and write about the places contained on the pages. Of course, some locations remain and some have disappeared or changed over the decades, but it can’t spoil the enjoyment of looking and hoping for a discovery. Here is Alder in Deauville: “Our tour starts on the Planches boardwalk, bordered on the beach side by multicoloured parasols and on the land side by the établissement des bains de mer , with sea-water bathing, thalassotherapy and spa facilities. Here, at the Bar du Soleil , in August 1931, Simenon signed copies of the first Maigret novels, an event commemorated by a plaque unveiled by the Municipal Council of Deauville on 23 August 2013. It is here, on the terrace of the bar, that Émile and Torrence settle down ‘in wicker armchairs […] to enjoy some really delicious cocktails’ (‘La Fleuriste de Deauville’, p. 328).” “Exploring Crime Fiction” has a photo of the signing session plaque. Alder also considers the importance of Normandy in Simenon’s early pulp fiction and the later non-Maigret novels. The Belgian author, born in Liège on February 13, 1903, honed his craft in the 1920s by writing more than 200 books of pulp fiction published under a variety of pseudonyms, 17 (or 16 or 18) of them by one count, and this occasional delve into that mostly lost but formative period is a further bonus for we Simenon enthusiasts. These are almost forgotten now and expensive if found. Fascinatingly, Alder drops in some facts and notes that Normandy is also a recurrent setting in both these early works and the subsequent non-Maigret narratives of the romans durs (“hard novels”) and short stories. These, he tells, stretch from the mid-1920s (“La Pucelle de Bénouville”/”The Virgin of Bénouville” in 1927) to “Les Anneaux de Bicêtre”/”The Bells of Bicêtre” in 1963), and, interestingly for this investigative author, Simenon’s Normandy settings are largely drawn from the region’s coastal ports and seaside resorts rather than the urban or rural interior. Many of their titles “give a strong flavour of their location’s maritime vocation by their inclusion of a place name or a reference to a boat”: La Pucelle de Bénouville”, “Au Rendez-vous des Terre-Neuvas”, “Le Port des brumes”, “L’Énigme de la Marie-Galante”/”The Mystery of the Marie-Galante”, “Les Rescapés du Télémaque”/”The Survivors”, “Le comique du Saint-Antoine”/”The Joker of the Saint-Antoine”, “Le vieux couple de Cherbourg”/”The Old Couple from Cherbourg”, “Le Fleuriste de Deauville”/”The Deauville Flower Seller”, “Tempête sur la Manche” and “Le bateau d’Émile”/”Émile’s Boat”). Alder notes that the action centres from Dieppe in the north of the département of Seine-Inférieure (currently Seine-Maritime) to Port-en-Bessin in the Calvados département, passing through Fécamp and Étretat in the Pays de Caux, between Dieppe and the estuary of the Seine, Ouistreham, where the river Orne and its adjacent canal meet the sea, and Deauville on the Côte Fleurie. Simenon went to Normandy for the first time in 1925 with his then wife Régine for a summer holiday in Bénouville, near Étretat, and the impact on him was instant. From the spring of 1928 onwards the Simenons spent almost six months on the rivers and canals of France on a tiny boat, the Ginette, after which he commissioned a Fécamp shipbuilder to construct a cutter, the Ostrogoth. From spring 1929 the Ostrogoth would be their home for two and a half years travelling the seas of northern Europe, and lead to the birth of Maigret, while the boat was laid up for recaulking, a moment Alder judges to be a turning point in the history of crime fiction. “Exploring Crime Fiction”, then, explores all this, examining the Normandy coast’s importance in Simenon’s personal and literary development. As Alder explains, by situating these works within their historical and social contexts, he can uncover the realities that shaped their creation and the broader questions they raise about 20 th -century crime fiction. His book combines literary analysis with guided tours of these six key locations, following the trail of Simenon’s characters through Bénouville and Étretat, Fécamp, Deauville, Ouistreham, Dieppe and Port-en-Bessin, thus highlighting their importance in Simenon’s storytelling and their role in shaping the genre of crime fiction. For fans of Simenon, for crime fiction enthusiasts and for readers intrigued by the interplay between literature and location, “Exploring Crime Fiction” comes with the promise of a unique perspective on Simenon’s work, blending historical insight with an immersive exploration of the landscapes that inspired the stories. Alder examines provincialism, narrative strategies and, for good measure, how these mysteries were adapted to cinema, television, radio and even strip cartoons. He also investigates translations from the French: should translators opt for authenticity of the original text or make slight changes to allow better accessibility for non-French readers? Bill Alder is an academic, a retired lecturer for the School of Languages and Applied Linguistics at Open University, United Kingdom. Crime fiction fans must appreciate this detailed critical analysis of and welcome addition to the many works of Georges Simenon and the books about him.
